title: Self-perceptions

paragraphs.text: The difference between how we see ourselves and how others see us is not just a matter of egocentrism. We all have misperceptions about ourselves, and we alter and update our self-image when we see ourselves through other eyes. Part of the discrepancy arises because an outsider's perspective affords information that we ourselves miss.

How well we understand ourselves has a profound impact on our ability to get along within our community. In some respects, we are so biased by our need to see ourselves in a good light that we become strangers to ourselves. We can learn more about ourselves and how we appear to others by asking for feedback from other people. To do this it is helpful to divide all the things that can be known about us into four categories.

First, there are 'bright spots' - attributes known by both ourselves and others. Studies show that traits like extroversion, talkativeness and dominance are easily observable both to self and others. Second are 'dark spots' - things known by neither ourselves nor others. These could include deep unconscious motives that drive our behaviours, such as the fact that a person's relentless ambition is driven by the need to prove her ability to her overly critical parents. Third are 'personal spots' - things known only by ourselves, like a dislike of our co-workers. And finally there are 'blind spots' - things known only by others, which can include such factors as our level of hostility and defensiveness, our attractiveness and our intelligence.

Of these four categories, the most interesting are the last two - personal spots and blind spots - since they involve discrepancies between how we see ourselves and how others see us. We are not entirely mistaken about ourselves: we do know what we like and what we believe about most things. And even if we don't know the mysterious unconscious motives underlying what we like and do, we are still the best source of information about our attitudes, beliefs and preferences.

We often think that other people are aware of our anxiety or our darkest feelings, but research by Terence Gulliver, a psychologist at Cornell University in the USA, shows that they are actually poor judges of our emotions, intentions and thoughts. Gulliver found that numerous obstacles and psychological biases obscure how we are seen by others. We overestimate the extent to which our internal states are detectable to others - a bias known as the illusion of transparency. It is also common to overestimate the extent to which our behaviour and appearance are observed and evaluated by others - a bias known as the spotlight effect.

We are good at judging our own self-esteem, optimism and pessimism and anything to do with our emotions. So for instance others may think someone is very calm, when in fact he is so nervous in large groups that his hands sweat and his heart races. These personal spots exist because others know how we behave, but they don't know our intentions or feelings, explains Sara Violetti, a researcher at Washington University in the USA. 'If you're quiet at a party, people don't know if it's because you're arrogant and you think you're better than everyone else, or because you're shy,' she says.

There are many reasons to think that we would be the best judge of ourselves. But we are very biased. We have a vested interest in seeing ourselves as decent and competent, and not evil or inept. When it comes to traits that matter to our self-esteem, we tend to have positive delusions - meaning that on these points, others see us more accurately than we see ourselves. 'It's difficult to rank your own intelligence,' explains Violetti. When people are asked to do this, their own ratings do not match their scores on IQ tests. But when the researchers ask other people to rate their friends' intelligence, they are actually fairly good judges. The same goes for honesty. Such positive delusions about ourselves function to boost our confidence and help us recover more quickly from rejection. Similarly, we are not aware of how attractive we are because it gives our ego a boost to believe in our own beauty.

We also only see ourselves through our own eyes, as in the case of body language, 'It's a matter of physical perspective,' explains Violetti. 'Your own body isn't in your field of sight. So in addition to the psychological advantage of being more objective, other people also have a physical advantage in detecting your behaviours.' If we do know how irritating or how likeable we are, it's probably through others close to us giving us direct or indirect feedback. Getting a different perspective actually provides you with new information. Richard Robbins of the University of California in the USA examined how people viewed their own contributions to a group discussion task. First, subjects were asked to rate how well they did. Then they watched a video of the discussion after which they downgraded their evaluations. There is much knowledge to be gained about ourselves and others by seeking other perspectives.
